questions.enonce_markdown: $\dfrac{1}{(x+1)(x^2-x+1)}$, $x \neq -1$, expressed in partial fractions where $A$, $B$ and $C$ are real constants, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The quadratic factor $x^2-x+1$ is irreducible over the reals (discriminant $(-1)^2-4=-3<0$), so its partial fraction needs a **linear** numerator $Bx+C$, while the linear factor $x+1$ needs a constant numerator $A$:

$$\frac{1}{(x+1)(x^2-x+1)}=\frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{Bx+C}{x^2-x+1}.$$

Check by finding the constants: $1=A(x^2-x+1)+(Bx+C)(x+1)$. Putting $x=-1$ gives $1=3A$, so $A=\tfrac13$. Comparing $x^2$: $A+B=0$, so $B=-\tfrac13$; comparing constants: $A+C=1$, so $C=\tfrac23$. The decomposition exists, which confirms the form.

Options B and C have numerators that are too restricted (a constant, or $Bx$ with no constant term); option D has two constants over the same denominator, which merge into one constant and cannot give the $x$ term. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The integrating factor for the differential equation $x^2\dfrac{dy}{dx}+4xy=e^x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Write the equation in the standard form $\dfrac{dy}{dx}+P(x)\,y=Q(x)$ by dividing by $x^2$ (for $x\neq 0$):

$$\frac{dy}{dx}+\frac{4}{x}\,y=\frac{e^x}{x^2}.$$

Here $P(x)=\dfrac4x$, so the integrating factor is
$$e^{\int P\,dx}=e^{4\ln|x|}=|x|^4=x^4.$$

Check: multiplying the original equation by $x^2$ gives $x^4\dfrac{dy}{dx}+4x^3y=\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^4y\right)=x^2e^x$, so the left side is an exact derivative. The trap is to read $P=4x$ without first dividing by $x^2$ (option A or B). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $f(x)=3\cosh 3x-2$, then the minimum value of $f(x)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For every real $u$, $\cosh u=\dfrac{e^u+e^{-u}}{2}\ge 1$, with equality only at $u=0$. Hence $\cosh 3x\ge 1$ and

$$f(x)=3\cosh 3x-2\ge 3(1)-2=1,$$

with equality at $x=0$. (Alternatively $f'(x)=9\sinh 3x=0$ at $x=0$ and $f''(0)=27>0$, a minimum.) The minimum value is $f(0)=1$. The trap is to use $\cosh 0=0$, which gives $-2$ (option A). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $y=|x|+x-x|x|$, if $x<0$, then $y=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
For $x<0$ we have $|x|=-x$, hence $x|x|=x(-x)=-x^2$. Therefore

$$y=|x|+x-x|x|=(-x)+x-(-x^2)=x^2.$$

Check with $x=-2$: $|{-2}|+(-2)-(-2)(2)=2-2+4=4=(-2)^2$. The trap is to replace $|x|$ by $x$ (giving option C or D). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The range of values of $x$ for which the Taylor's expansion about $x=0$ of $\ln\left(\dfrac{1-2x}{(1+2x)^2}\right)$ is valid is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Split the logarithm:

$$\ln\frac{1-2x}{(1+2x)^2}=\ln(1-2x)-2\ln(1+2x).$$

The Maclaurin series of $\ln(1+u)$ is valid for $-1<u\le 1$.

- $\ln(1+2x)$: $u=2x$, so $-1<2x\le1$, that is $-\tfrac12<x\le\tfrac12$.
- $\ln(1-2x)$: $u=-2x$, so $-1<-2x\le 1$, that is $-\tfrac12\le x<\tfrac12$.

The expansion of the whole expression is valid only where **both** series converge, i.e. on the intersection $-\tfrac12<x<\tfrac12$. Each endpoint is excluded by one of the two series (at $x=\tfrac12$ the factor $1-2x$ vanishes and $\ln 0$ is undefined; at $x=-\tfrac12$ the factor $1+2x$ vanishes). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The conjugate of the complex number $1+e^{i\theta}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For real $\theta$, $e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta$ has conjugate $\cos\theta-i\sin\theta=e^{-i\theta}$. The real number $1$ is its own conjugate, and the conjugate of a sum is the sum of the conjugates, so

$$\overline{1+e^{i\theta}}=1+e^{-i\theta}.$$

Only the imaginary part changes sign: the sign in front of the exponential does not (options B and C). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Given the truth table below

| $p$ | $q$ | $p\lor q$ | $(p\lor q)\Rightarrow q$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| T | T | T | T |
| T | F | a | T |
| F | T | T | T |
| F | F | F | b |

The truth values of a and b are respectively
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **a** is $p\lor q$ in the row $p=T,\ q=F$. A disjunction is true when at least one part is true, so $T\lor F=T$. Hence $a=T$.
- **b** is $(p\lor q)\Rightarrow q$ in the row $p=F,\ q=F$. Here $p\lor q=F$ and $q=F$, so the statement is $F\Rightarrow F$. An implication is false only when the premise is true and the conclusion false; with a false premise it is true. Hence $b=T$.

So $(a,b)=(T,T)$. (The common error is to take $F\Rightarrow F$ as false.) **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
To establish a reduction formula for the integration of $\tan^n\theta$, it can be expressed as;

*Options as printed:* A) $\displaystyle\int \sec\theta\tan^{n}\theta\,d\theta$   B) $\displaystyle\int \tan\theta\tan^{n-1}\theta\,d\theta$   C) $\displaystyle\int \tan^{2}\theta\tan^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta$   D) $\displaystyle\int \sec\theta\tan^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The standard route to the reduction formula for $I_n=\displaystyle\int\tan^n\theta\,d\theta$ is to split off $\tan^2\theta$:

$$I_n=\int\tan^2\theta\,\tan^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta=\int(\sec^2\theta-1)\tan^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta=\frac{\tan^{n-1}\theta}{n-1}-I_{n-2}.$$

Option C is exactly this first step, $\tan^n\theta=\tan^2\theta\tan^{n-2}\theta$. Options A and D contain a factor $\sec\theta$ that is not in the integrand, so they are different integrals. **Note on the printed options:** option B, $\tan\theta\tan^{n-1}\theta$, is also identically equal to $\tan^n\theta$; it is simply not the useful split, because it does not introduce $\sec^2\theta$. The intended answer is C.

**Intended answer: C ($\displaystyle\int \tan^{2}\theta\tan^{n-2}\theta\,d\theta$).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The root mean square value of $\dfrac{1}{x}$ in the interval $1\le x\le 4$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The root mean square value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^b f(x)^2\,dx}$. Here $f(x)=\dfrac1x$, so $f^2=\dfrac1{x^2}$ and

$$\text{RMS}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4-1}\int_1^4\frac{dx}{x^2}}=\sqrt{\frac13\left[-\frac1x\right]_1^4}=\sqrt{\frac13\left(1-\frac14\right)}=\sqrt{\frac14}=\frac12.$$

Options A and C come from integrating $\dfrac1x$ (a logarithm) instead of $\dfrac1{x^2}$. **Answer: B.**
themes: mean and root mean square values

questions.enonce_markdown: The polar equation of the curve $x^2+y^2=2x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$ and $x^2+y^2=r^2$:

$$r^2=2r\cos\theta\ \Longrightarrow\ r=2\cos\theta\quad(r\neq0),$$

and the pole $r=0$ is included in the curve (at $\theta=\tfrac\pi2$). This is the circle of centre $(1,0)$ and radius $1$. Option A has $r^2$ on the left and the cosine without the factor $r$, which is the common slip; options B and C use $\sin\theta$, which would give a circle centred on the $y$-axis. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The coordinates of the focus of the parabola $x^2=16(y+1)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compare with $X^2=4aY$ where $X=x$ and $Y=y+1$. Then $4a=16$, so $a=4$. In the $(X,Y)$ frame the vertex is at the origin and the focus at $(0,a)=(0,4)$. Since $Y=y+1$, the vertex is at $(0,-1)$ in the original axes and the focus is at

$$(0,\,-1+4)=(0,3).$$

The trap is to forget the shift $y+1$ and give $(0,4)$ (option B). **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $(\lambda\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{k})\times(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}-\mathbf{k})=-4\mathbf{i}+8\mathbf{j}-16\mathbf{k}$, the value of $\lambda$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Compute the vector product with $\mathbf a=(\lambda,0,-4)$ and $\mathbf b=(2,-1,-1)$:

$$\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\begin{vmatrix}\mathbf i&\mathbf j&\mathbf k\\ \lambda&0&-4\\ 2&-1&-1\end{vmatrix}=\bigl(0\cdot(-1)-(-4)(-1)\bigr)\mathbf i-\bigl(\lambda(-1)-(-4)(2)\bigr)\mathbf j+\bigl(\lambda(-1)-0\cdot2\bigr)\mathbf k$$

$$=-4\mathbf i+(\lambda-8)\mathbf j-\lambda\mathbf k.$$

Equating with $-4\mathbf i+8\mathbf j-16\mathbf k$: the $\mathbf i$ components agree ($-4$); $\lambda-8=8$ gives $\lambda=16$; and $-\lambda=-16$ gives $\lambda=16$. Both components give the same value, so $\lambda=16$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\begin{vmatrix}1&1&4\\3&5&1\\1&2&0\end{vmatrix}=3$, then $\begin{vmatrix}3&5&1\\1&1&4\\1&2&0\end{vmatrix}=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The second determinant is the first with rows 1 and 2 **interchanged** (row 1 is now $(3,5,1)$, row 2 is $(1,1,4)$, row 3 is unchanged). Interchanging two rows multiplies a determinant by $-1$, so its value is $-3$.

Check by direct expansion of the first determinant along row 1: $1(0-2)-1(0-1)+4(6-5)=-2+1+4=3$, and of the second: $3(0-8)-5(0-4)+1(2-1)=-24+20+1=-3$. **Answer: A.**

The identity $e$ satisfies $e*g=g*e=g$ for every $g$ in the set. So its row must repeat the column headings and its column must repeat the row headings.

Look at the last row: $x^4*x=x$, $x^4*x^2=x^2$, $x^4*x^3=x^3$, $x^4*x^4=x^4$. It reproduces the heading $x,x^2,x^3,x^4$, and the last column does the same ($x*x^4=x$, $x^2*x^4=x^2$, ...). Hence the identity is $x^4$ (the group is cyclic of order 4 with generator $x$, and $x*x^4=x$ confirms that $x^4$ plays the role of "$x^0$"). The element $x$ is a generator, not the identity, since $x*x=x^2\neq x$. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which one of the following linear congruencies has no solution?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The congruence $ax\equiv b\pmod n$ has a solution if and only if $\gcd(a,n)$ divides $b$. Here $a=15$, $b=6$:

- $\gcd(15,21)=3$, and $3\mid 6$: solutions exist.
- $\gcd(15,40)=5$, and $5\nmid 6$: **no solution**.
- $\gcd(15,36)=3$, and $3\mid 6$: solutions exist.
- $\gcd(15,81)=3$, and $3\mid 6$: solutions exist.

Check for modulus 40: $15x-40k$ is always a multiple of $5$, so it can never equal $6$. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: All the asymptotes to the curve $y=f(x)$, where $f(x)=x+1+\ln\left|\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}\right|$, are
questions.corrige_markdown:
- **Vertical asymptotes.** As $x\to-1$ the denominator $x+1\to0$, so $\left|\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}\right|\to\infty$ and $f\to+\infty$: $x=-1$ is an asymptote. As $x\to-2$ the numerator $x+2\to0$, so the logarithm tends to $-\infty$: $x=-2$ is an asymptote too.
- **Oblique asymptote.** As $x\to\pm\infty$, $\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}=1+\dfrac1{x+1}\to1$, so $\ln\left|\dfrac{x+2}{x+1}\right|\to\ln1=0$ and $f(x)-(x+1)\to0$. Hence $y=x+1$ is an asymptote at both ends.

All three lines are asymptotes, and the question asks for **all** of them. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If $P$ and $Q$ are statements, then $\sim(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $P\Rightarrow Q\equiv\ \sim P\lor Q$. Then, by De Morgan's law,

$$\sim(P\Rightarrow Q)\equiv\ \sim(\sim P\lor Q)\equiv\ \sim\sim P\land\sim Q\equiv P\land\sim Q.$$

In words: an implication fails exactly when the premise is true and the conclusion is false. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=\begin{cases}\tfrac12x^2, & 0\le x<2\\ cx+3, & 2\le x\le5\end{cases}$. The value of $c$ for which $f$ is continuous in $0\le x\le5$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Each piece is a polynomial, hence continuous on its own interval; the only point to check is $x=2$, where the formula changes.

- Left limit: $\displaystyle\lim_{x\to2^-}\tfrac12x^2=\tfrac12(4)=2$.
- Value and right limit: $f(2)=2c+3$.

Continuity requires $2c+3=2$, so $c=-\dfrac12$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $x$ for which $\cosh^{-1}(2x)=\ln 4$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take $\cosh$ of both sides: $2x=\cosh(\ln 4)=\dfrac{e^{\ln4}+e^{-\ln4}}{2}=\dfrac{4+\tfrac14}{2}=\dfrac{17}{8}$.

Hence $x=\dfrac{17}{16}$. (Cross-check with $\cosh^{-1}u=\ln\left(u+\sqrt{u^2-1}\right)$: for $u=\tfrac{17}{8}$, $\sqrt{\tfrac{289}{64}-1}=\tfrac{15}{8}$, and $\tfrac{17}{8}+\tfrac{15}{8}=4$, so the logarithm is $\ln4$ as required.) The trap is to stop at $2x=\tfrac{17}{8}$ (option D) or to use $\sinh$ (giving $\tfrac{15}{16}$). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A similarity transformation (similitude) $f$, on a complex plane is defined by $z'=(1+i)z+3-4i$. Its scale factor is
questions.corrige_markdown:
A direct similarity of the complex plane has the form $z'=az+b$. It is a rotation through $\arg a$ combined with an enlargement of scale factor $|a|$ (and a translation by $b$). Here $a=1+i$, so

$$\text{scale factor}=|1+i|=\sqrt{1^2+1^2}=\sqrt2,$$

and the rotation angle is $\arg(1+i)=\tfrac\pi4$. The number $5=|3-4i|$ belongs to the translation part and does not affect the scale. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^7-x^5+\frac{\sin x}{(1+x^4)^2}\right)dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Over a symmetric interval $[-a,a]$, the integral of an **odd** function is zero. Each term is odd:

- $x^7$ and $x^5$ are odd powers;
- $\dfrac{\sin x}{(1+x^4)^2}$ is odd, because $\sin x$ is odd and $(1+x^4)^2$ is even.

So the integrand $g$ satisfies $g(-x)=-g(x)$ and $\displaystyle\int_{-1}^1 g\,dx=0$. No integration is needed. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The general solution of the differential equation $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}+4x=0$, where $p$ and $q$ are constants is $x=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The auxiliary equation is $m^2+4=0$, so $m=\pm2i$. With purely imaginary roots there is no exponential factor, and the general solution is

$$x=A\cos2t+B\sin2t=p\cos(2t+\lambda),$$

where $p=\sqrt{A^2+B^2}$ is the amplitude and $\lambda$ a phase constant (two arbitrary constants, as required for a second order equation). Options A and B contain $e^t$, which would need a real part in the roots; option D has angular frequency $4$ instead of $\sqrt4=2$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The mean value of the function $\ln x$ in the interval $1\le x\le e$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The mean value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\dfrac1{b-a}\displaystyle\int_a^bf(x)\,dx$. Using $\displaystyle\int\ln x\,dx=x\ln x-x$:

$$\int_1^e\ln x\,dx=\bigl[x\ln x-x\bigr]_1^e=(e-e)-(0-1)=1.$$

Therefore the mean value is $\dfrac{1}{e-1}\times1=\dfrac1{e-1}\approx0.582$. The trap is to forget the division by the length $e-1$ of the interval (the integral alone is $1$). **Answer: D.**
themes: mean and root mean square values

questions.enonce_markdown: A curve is given in Cartesian form by the equation $x^2+y^2-2x=(x^2+y^2)^{\frac12}$. The polar equation of the curve is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Substitute $x=r\cos\theta$, $x^2+y^2=r^2$ and $(x^2+y^2)^{1/2}=r$ (taking $r\ge0$):

$$r^2-2r\cos\theta=r\ \Longrightarrow\ r-2\cos\theta=1\quad(r\neq0)\ \Longrightarrow\ r=1+2\cos\theta.$$

This is a limaçon. Check with $\theta=0$: $r=3$, the point $(3,0)$, and $9-6=3=\sqrt9$, which satisfies the Cartesian equation. The $\cos\theta$ (not $\sin\theta$) comes from the term $-2x$, and the sign of $2\cos\theta$ comes from moving $r$ to the other side. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If the asymptotes of the hyperbola $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1$ are perpendicular, then the value of $a$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The asymptotes of $\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ are $y=\pm\dfrac bax$. Here $b^2=16$, so $b=4$ and the slopes are $\pm\dfrac4a$.

Two lines are perpendicular when the product of their slopes is $-1$:

$$\frac4a\times\left(-\frac4a\right)=-\frac{16}{a^2}=-1\ \Longrightarrow\ a^2=16\ \Longrightarrow\ a=4\quad(a>0).$$

Equivalently the hyperbola is rectangular ($a=b$). **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are two vectors, which one of the following compound statements is true?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\sin\theta\,\hat{\mathbf n}$.

- **A is true.** Parallel vectors have $\theta=0$ or $\pi$, so $\sin\theta=0$ and $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\mathbf 0$.
- B is false: perpendicular vectors give $\sin\theta=\pm1$, so $|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=|\mathbf a||\mathbf b|\neq0$ for non-zero vectors.
- C is false: $\mathbf i\times\mathbf j=\mathbf k=\mathbf j\times(-\mathbf i)$, yet $\mathbf a=\mathbf i\neq\mathbf c=\mathbf j$.
- D is false: $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b$ is always perpendicular to $\mathbf a$, never parallel to it (unless it is the zero vector).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: $\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=\mathbf c\times\mathbf d\Rightarrow\mathbf a=\mathbf c$ and $\mathbf b=\mathbf d$
$\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\parallel\mathbf a$ if $\mathbf a\perp\mathbf b$

questions.enonce_markdown: For what value of $p$ is the matrix $\begin{pmatrix}p&5&6\\4&3&3\\6&7&9\end{pmatrix}$ non-invertible?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A square matrix is non-invertible exactly when its determinant is zero. Expand along the first row:

$$\det=p(3\cdot9-3\cdot7)-5(4\cdot9-3\cdot6)+6(4\cdot7-3\cdot6)=p(6)-5(18)+6(10)=6p-90+60=6p-30.$$

Setting $6p-30=0$ gives $p=5$. Check: for $p=0$ the determinant is $-30$, for $p=7$ it is $12$ and for $p=9$ it is $24$, all non-zero. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A necessary and sufficient condition to show that a group is Abelian is
questions.corrige_markdown: By definition, a group $(G,*)$ is **Abelian** (commutative) when $a*b=b*a$ for all $a,b\in G$. Closure, associativity, the existence of an identity and of inverses are the axioms that every group satisfies, Abelian or not, so they cannot distinguish an Abelian group from another group (for instance $S_3$ satisfies all of them but is not Abelian). The extra condition that is both necessary and sufficient is therefore commutativity. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The number of solutions to the congruence $6x\equiv15\pmod{21}$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $d=\gcd(6,21)=3$. Since $3\mid15$, the congruence is solvable, and it then has exactly $d=3$ incongruent solutions modulo $21$.

Explicitly, divide by $3$: $2x\equiv5\pmod7$. Since $2\times4=8\equiv1\pmod7$, the inverse of $2$ is $4$, so $x\equiv20\equiv6\pmod7$. The solutions modulo $21$ are $x\equiv6,\ 13,\ 20$. Check: $6\times6=36\equiv15$, $6\times13=78=3\times21+15$, $6\times20=120=5\times21+15$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The solutions of $z^3=8$ are $z=$
The general solution to the differential equation $3\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}-4\dfrac{dy}{dx}=0$, for constants $A$, $B$ is $y=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
The auxiliary equation is $3m^2-4m=0$, that is $m(3m-4)=0$, so $m=0$ or $m=\dfrac43$. Two distinct real roots give

$$y=Ae^{0\cdot x}+Be^{\frac43x}=A+Be^{\frac43x}.$$

Check: $y'=\tfrac43Be^{4x/3}$, $y''=\tfrac{16}9Be^{4x/3}$, and $3y''-4y'=\tfrac{16}3Be^{4x/3}-\tfrac{16}3Be^{4x/3}=0$. The factor $x$ in A and C is only needed for a repeated root; D inverts the fraction. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: For any constant $k$, $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-9}}\,dx=$
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the standard result $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2-a^2}}=\cosh^{-1}\left(\frac xa\right)+k$ for $x>a$ (equivalently $\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2-a^2}\right)+k'$), here with $a=3$.

Check by differentiating: $\dfrac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1}\dfrac x3=\dfrac{1/3}{\sqrt{(x/3)^2-1}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x^2-9}}$. The other inverse functions belong to different integrands: $\sin^{-1}$ and $\cos^{-1}$ to $\sqrt{9-x^2}$, and $\sinh^{-1}$ to $\sqrt{x^2+9}$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equation $\dfrac{x^2}{2-a}+\dfrac{y^2}{a-5}=-1$ represents an ellipse if
questions.corrige_markdown:
Multiply by $-1$:

$$\frac{x^2}{a-2}+\frac{y^2}{5-a}=1.$$

This is an ellipse when both denominators are positive: $a-2>0$ and $5-a>0$, that is $2<a<5$ (the value $a=\tfrac72$ gives equal denominators, a circle, which is a special ellipse). If $a<2$ both denominators are negative and the left side cannot equal $1$ (no curve); if $a>5$ the denominators have opposite signs and the curve is a hyperbola. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\2&3&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $N=\begin{pmatrix}1&2&3\\3&2&1\end{pmatrix}$ are elements of $S_3$, the symmetric group of permutations of $A=\{1,2,3\}$, the composition $M\circ N=$

The rate of cooling of a liquid is proportional to the difference between its temperature, $\theta$ and the temperature of the room $\alpha$. The differential equation which models this process, for some positive $k$, is
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is Newton's law of cooling. A hot liquid ($\theta>\alpha$) loses temperature, so $\dfrac{d\theta}{dt}<0$ when $\theta-\alpha>0$. With a **positive** constant $k$ we therefore need a minus sign:

$$\frac{d\theta}{dt}=-k(\theta-\alpha).$$

Option A has no constant of proportionality; B would make the liquid heat up; D, $-k(\alpha-\theta)=k(\theta-\alpha)$, is the same as B. The solution is $\theta=\alpha+(\theta_0-\alpha)e^{-kt}$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Using the approximation $y_{n+1}\cong y_n+h\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)_n$ and a step length of $0.2$, the approximate value of $y$, when $x=1.2$, given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ and $y=0$ when $x=1$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
This is Euler's method with $h=0.2$, starting at $(x_0,y_0)=(1,0)$. Going from $x=1$ to $x=1.2$ is exactly **one** step:

$$y_1=y_0+h\,(x_0+y_0)=0+0.2(1+0)=0.2.$$

So $y(1.2)\approx0.2$. The values $1.2$ and $1.4$ come from using the wrong starting values or from forgetting the factor $h$; $1.68$ would need further steps. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle performing simple harmonic motion has a speed of $4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ when it is $1\ \mathrm m$ from the centre of oscillations. If the period of oscillations is $\sqrt2\pi\ \mathrm s$, its amplitude is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For SHM, $v^2=\omega^2(a^2-x^2)$ and $T=\dfrac{2\pi}{\omega}$. With $T=\sqrt2\,\pi$:

$$\omega=\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt2\,\pi}=\sqrt2,\qquad\omega^2=2.$$

Substitute $v=4$ and $x=1$: $16=2(a^2-1)$, so $a^2-1=8$, $a^2=9$ and $a=3\ \mathrm m$. Check: $v^2=2(9-1)=16$. **Answer: B.**
themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle

questions.enonce_markdown: The moment of inertia of a uniform rod of mass $2m$ and length $l$ about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to the rod is
questions.corrige_markdown:
For a uniform rod of mass $M$ and length $l$, the moment of inertia about a perpendicular axis through its centre is $\dfrac1{12}Ml^2$. Here $M=2m$:

$$I=\frac1{12}(2m)l^2=\frac16ml^2.$$

(Derivation: $I=\displaystyle\int_{-l/2}^{l/2}\frac{M}{l}x^2\,dx=\frac Ml\cdot\frac{2}{3}\left(\frac l2\right)^3=\frac{Ml^2}{12}$.) The trap is to use the value $\tfrac13Ml^2$ about an end, or to forget that the mass is $2m$. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The line of action of a force $\mathbf F$ with point of application $P$, such that $\overrightarrow{OP}=\mathbf r$ is $\mathbf r+\lambda\mathbf F$. Which one of the following statements is NOT true?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The moment of a force about $O$ is $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ for **any** point with position vector $\mathbf r$ on the line of action.

- A is true (definition of the moment about $O$).
- B is true: $(\mathbf r+\lambda\mathbf F)\times\mathbf F=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F+\lambda(\mathbf F\times\mathbf F)=\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$, because $\mathbf F\times\mathbf F=\mathbf 0$. Sliding the point along the line of action does not change the moment.
- **C is NOT true**: since the two vectors are equal (statement B), one cannot be less than the other.
- D is true: relative to the point $\mathbf a$ the position vector of $P$ is $\mathbf r-\mathbf a$.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: $\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ is the moment of $\mathbf F$ about $O$
$\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ is equal to $(\mathbf r+\lambda\mathbf F)\times\mathbf F$
$\mathbf r\times\mathbf F$ is less than $(\mathbf r+\lambda\mathbf F)\times\mathbf F$
$(\mathbf r-\mathbf a)\times\mathbf F$ is the moment of $\mathbf F$ about the point with position vector $\mathbf a$.

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle $P$ moves with constant angular speed $\omega$ on a curve whose polar equation is $r=(1+\cos\theta)$, the traverse component of its acceleration is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The transverse component of acceleration is $a_\theta=r\ddot\theta+2\dot r\dot\theta$. With constant angular speed, $\dot\theta=\omega$ and $\ddot\theta=0$, so $a_\theta=2\dot r\omega$.

Differentiate $r=1+\cos\theta$: $\dot r=-\sin\theta\,\dot\theta=-\omega\sin\theta$. Therefore

$$a_\theta=2(-\omega\sin\theta)\,\omega=-2\omega^2\sin\theta.$$

The dimensions confirm it: an acceleration has the dimension of $\omega^2\times$ length, ruling out A and B, which carry only one power of $\omega$. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
When two elastic objects collide obliquely, which one of the following statements is NOT true?

*Options as printed:* A) Their velocities perpendicular to the line of centres do not change   B) They move in opposite directions after impact   C) Equal and opposite impulses act on each of them   D) The total kinetic energy sometimes decreases.
questions.corrige_markdown:
For smooth objects colliding obliquely, resolve the velocities along and perpendicular to the line of centres.

- A is true: the impulse acts along the line of centres only, so the perpendicular components are unchanged.
- C is true: by Newton's third law the impulses are equal and opposite.
- **B is NOT true in general**: along the line of centres the relative velocity is reversed (scaled by $e$), but each object keeps its unchanged perpendicular component, and a heavy object may continue in its original direction. The objects need not move in opposite directions after impact.
- D: kinetic energy is conserved for perfectly elastic objects ($e=1$) and decreases when $e<1$, so the wording ("sometimes decreases") is not a precise statement either way.

The intended answer is B.

**Intended answer: B (They move in opposite directions after impact).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The value of $k$ for which $p(x)=\begin{cases}k(x+2), & x=0,1,2,3,4\\ 0, & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$ is a discrete probability density function is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The probabilities of a discrete distribution must sum to $1$:

$$\sum_{x=0}^4k(x+2)=k(2+3+4+5+6)=20k=1\ \Longrightarrow\ k=\frac1{20}.$$

All values $p(x)=\dfrac{x+2}{20}$ are positive, so $p$ is a valid probability function. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A liquid is leaking from a container at the rate of $\dfrac2x$ litres per second where $x$ is the quantity in litres, of liquid remaining in the container after time $t$ seconds. If initially there are 20 litres of liquid in the container, the time in which the quantity of the liquid reduces from 20 litres to 10 litres in seconds is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The quantity decreases, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-\dfrac2x$. Separate the variables:

$$\int x\,dx=-2\int dt\ \Longrightarrow\ \frac{x^2}2=-2t+C.$$

At $t=0$, $x=20$: $200=C$. Then $x=10$ gives $50=-2t+200$, so $t=75$ seconds. Check: a time is positive; the negative values $-125$ and $-75$ come from a sign error. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Given that $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=x+y$ and $y=1$ when $x=0$, the first three terms in the series expansion of $y$ in ascending powers of $x$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Use the Maclaurin series $y=y(0)+xy'(0)+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}y''(0)+\cdots$.

- $y(0)=1$.
- $y'=x+y$, so $y'(0)=0+1=1$.
- Differentiating, $y''=1+y'$, so $y''(0)=1+1=2$.

Hence $y=1+x+\dfrac{2}{2}x^2+\cdots=1+x+x^2+\cdots$

Check against the exact solution $y=2e^x-x-1=1+x+x^2+\tfrac{x^3}3+\cdots$. The error in option A is to forget the $y'$ term when differentiating $y'=x+y$ a second time. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle oscillates through a distance $0.4\ m$ on either side of its equilibrium position with period of 4 seconds. The maximum speed of the particle is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The amplitude is $a=0.4\ \mathrm m$ (the distance on either side of the equilibrium position), and $\omega=\dfrac{2\pi}{T}=\dfrac{2\pi}4=\dfrac\pi2\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}}$.

The maximum speed in SHM occurs at the centre and equals $a\omega$:

$$v_{\max}=0.4\times\frac\pi2=0.2\pi\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\approx0.628\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}.$$

The trap is to use $\omega=\pi$ (option D, which corresponds to a period of 2 s). **Answer: A.**
themes: simple harmonic motion of a particle

questions.enonce_markdown: If the moment of inertia of a square lamina of side $a$ and mass $m$ about an axis through its centre and perpendicular to its plane is $I$, then its moment of inertia about an axis through an edge in the plane of the lamina is
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. **Perpendicular axes theorem.** Let $I_x$ and $I_y$ be the moments of inertia about the two axes through the centre, in the plane and parallel to the sides. By symmetry $I_x=I_y$, and $I=I_x+I_y$, so $I_x=\dfrac12I$.
2. **Parallel axes theorem.** The edge is parallel to one of these axes at distance $\dfrac a2$, so
$$I_{\text{edge}}=I_x+m\left(\frac a2\right)^2=\frac12I+\frac14ma^2.$$

Check with $I=\dfrac16ma^2$: $\tfrac1{12}ma^2+\tfrac14ma^2=\tfrac13ma^2$, the known value for a uniform square lamina about an edge. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A force $\mathbf F=(2\mathbf i+\mathbf j+\mathbf k)\ \mathrm N$ acts on a particle giving it a displacement of $(\mathbf i+\mathbf j+2\mathbf k)\ \mathrm m$. The work done by $\mathbf F$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Work done is the scalar product of force and displacement:

$$W=\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf d=(2)(1)+(1)(1)+(1)(2)=2+1+2=5\ \mathrm J.$$

Here $|\mathbf F|=|\mathbf d|=\sqrt6$, so $|\mathbf F||\mathbf d|=6$ is the maximum possible work, and $\sqrt{35}$ is not a possible value. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A particle is moving round the polar curve $r=a\cos\theta$ with constant angular velocity $\omega$. The transverse component of its velocity when $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$ is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The velocity in polar components is $\mathbf v=\dot r\,\hat{\mathbf r}+r\dot\theta\,\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$, so the transverse component is $v_\theta=r\dot\theta=r\omega$.

At $\theta=\dfrac\pi3$: $r=a\cos\dfrac\pi3=\dfrac a2$, hence $v_\theta=\dfrac12a\omega$. The radial component $\dot r=-a\omega\sin\theta$ is a different component and should not be used here (its magnitude at $\theta=\tfrac\pi3$ is $\tfrac{\sqrt3}2a\omega$, which is option B). **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A smooth sphere moving in space impinges on a similar sphere and its velocity changes from $(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-\mathbf k)\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. The direction of the line of centres is
questions.corrige_markdown:
The spheres are smooth, so the impulse acts along the line of centres only. The change of velocity of the sphere is therefore parallel to the line of centres:

$$\Delta\mathbf v=(3\mathbf i+\mathbf j-\mathbf k)-(2\mathbf i-\mathbf j+3\mathbf k)=\mathbf i+2\mathbf j-4\mathbf k.$$

The direction of a line has no sign, and $(-\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)=-\Delta\mathbf v$ is parallel to it. Option C, $(\mathbf i-2\mathbf j+4\mathbf k)$, is not parallel to $\Delta\mathbf v$ (it has the wrong sign on the $\mathbf j$ component), and A and D are the sum and the final velocity, which have no reason to lie along the line. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The equivalent of $P(|z|>a)$ is
questions.corrige_markdown:
Here $z$ is a standard normal variable with distribution function $\Phi$, and $a>0$. By the symmetry of the density about $0$:

$$P(|z|>a)=P(z>a)+P(z<-a)=2P(z>a)=2\bigl(1-\Phi(a)\bigr).$$

Option A is $P(|z|<a)$, the complementary probability; D is only one tail; C is negative for $a>0$ and so cannot be a probability. Numerical check with $a=1.3$: $2(1-\Phi(1.3))\approx0.1936$. **Answer: B.**
